clue.text: Curtail relaxation that includes brief prank

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: rest is relaxation

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a trick is a prank; shortened it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone wants to cut short a break that includes a quick practical joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like it describes the prank's length; it tells you to drop the final letter before the shortened word goes inside the relaxation.
explanation.definitionFit: To curtail something is to limit or cut it back, which is what restricting does.

clue.text: Leaves, getting reprimand

definitions.note: plural leaves for a salad plant named as a mass noun
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the peppery salad plant, also called arugula
second meaning: British slang for a severe telling-off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as a verb, someone departing; it is the salad. In British slang, to 'get a rocket' is to be told off sharply.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocket is a salad green eaten as leaves, and a rocket is also informal British speech for a stern scolding.

clue.text: Turns down incentives including bit of nepotism

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so one piece is set inside another

parts.note: spurs are incentives or stimuli

indicators.note: a bit is a small part, here just the opening letter of the word

parts.note: the first letter of nepotism

explanation.surface: Someone honest refuses perks that involve a little favouritism towards relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside SPURS, just before its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn is to reject or refuse with contempt, the same as turning an offer down.

clue.text: Resort with Everyman, from the outset, nagging people to fix things

parts.note: to repair to a place is to resort to it, go there
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as me

indicators.note: the outset is the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the first letter of nagging

explanation.surface: A holiday resort, the setter, and someone nagging tradesmen to get on with the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a noun, a holiday spot; here it is the old verb, as in 'repair to the drawing room'. A setter's own pen-name stands for ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Repairmen are workers whose job is mending broken appliances and equipment, so they are folk hired to fix things.

clue.text: 'We're N.I.C.E. Health questionable? Exercise!'

indicators.note: something questionable is doubtful or not right, so the letters are not in their right order

parts.note: all fourteen letters, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: A health body insists it is nice, then, doubted, barks an order to go and exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: NICE is Britain's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which advises on treatments. The dots make it look like an acronym, but its letters join the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A catherine-wheel is another name for a cartwheel, the gymnastic move of turning sideways over the hands, so it is a physical workout move.

clue.text: Wholesaler offloading dodgy sole; I'm seeking something more substantial

definitions.note: a clause spoken by the answer, not a noun phrase

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or not straight, so these letters appear in a jumbled order
to offload is to get rid of a load, so letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; jumbled it matches the run O, L, E, S inside the longer word

explanation.surface: A fish trader dumps some iffy sole, saying he wants something with more meat on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove OLES, a scramble of SOLE, from WHOLESALER to leave WHALER. The definition is the answer speaking: a sole is a small flatfish, and the whaler hunts much bigger prey.
explanation.definitionFit: A whaler is a person or ship that hunts whales, creatures vastly bigger than a flatfish, so its catch is weightier.

clue.text: Believer in growth industries, partly

indicators.note: partly means only in part, so the answer is a stretch of the text rather than whole words

parts.note: the end of growth runs into the start of industries

explanation.surface: An economist who has faith that certain sectors will expand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Believer in growth industries' reads as one phrase; 'in' is only the link between the definition and the words that hold the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu is a follower of Hinduism, a major world religion, so is a person of religious faith.

clue.text: Lazy type rising, transfixed by a TV showing foreign nationals

indicators.note: to be transfixed is to be pierced through, so one piece is driven into the other
in a down entry, rising means reading upward, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a snail is proverbially slow and idle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A couch potato gets up, spellbound by the television set.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAIL upside down is LIANS, and A TV goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvians are citizens of Latvia, a Baltic country, so to a British setter they are people from abroad.

clue.text: Regretted sports lesson having torn around centre field in the end

indicators.note: in the end means finally, so the last letter of the word is added at the close
around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: rent is an old past participle of rend, to tear
PE is physical education, the school sports lesson

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, which is the one kept

parts.note: the middle letter of field
the last letter of field

explanation.surface: A pupil regrets the games lesson where they tore around the middle of the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn around' reads as a pupil running about, but 'torn' is the old past participle of rend, and it goes around the sports lesson. 'Field' then gives both its centre and its end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To repent is to feel sorrow or remorse for something done, the same as regretting it.

clue.text: One that'll go off, but won't hit the roof?

definitions.text: One that'll go off, but won't hit the roof?

parts.words: One that'll go off, but won't hit the roof?
parts.note: surface reading: someone who loses their temper, yet somehow never flies into a rage

parts.words: One that'll go off, but won't hit the roof?
parts.note: setter's reading: a small explosive made to be set off inside, which never shoots up to the ceiling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' and 'hit the roof' are both idioms for losing your temper, so the clue seems to describe a person. Taken literally, it is a novelty firework for use indoors, which fizzes but does not launch.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a device ignites and pops like any explosive novelty, but is designed for use in a room, so nothing rockets upward.

clue.text: Cold blast, heading off for hot buttered food?

indicators.note: with its heading taken off, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
to trumpet is to blast out a loud sound; without its first letter it becomes RUMPET

explanation.surface: A chilly gust makes someone set off home for something warm and buttery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' looks like leaving; it tells you to drop the T of TRUMPET. A crumpet is a British griddle cake with holes on top, toasted and buttered.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumpets are spongy griddle cakes that are toasted and eaten warm, spread with butter that soaks into the holes.

clue.text: 24/7 drama, two Poles given crown

parts.note: No, also spelt Noh, is classical Japanese theatre
N and S, north and south, are the two poles
the crown of something is its top

explanation.surface: A round-the-clock soap opera in which two Polish characters are crowned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; it means the compass poles. The 'drama' is the Japanese form No.
explanation.definitionFit: 24/7 means twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, so continuous without any break.

clue.text: Weariness concerning, you and I said

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the words count by their sound rather than their spelling

parts.note: on means concerning, and we means you and I; run together they sound like the French word

explanation.surface: Someone admits that the two of us are getting tired.
explanation.walkthrough: Said with a French lilt, 'on we' gives the borrowed word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is a listless boredom and lack of interest, a kind of mental tiredness borrowed from French.

clue.text: No, outlive inferior — as part of this?

definitions.text: No, outlive inferior — as part of this?

indicators.note: inferior means poor or substandard, so these letters are in a worse, disordered state

parts.note: all nine letters of the two words

explanation.surface: The weaker ones don't survive, and that is part of the process.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read plainly it says the inferior do not outlive the fitter, which is natural selection.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Darwin's theory of evolution, weaker creatures die out while better-adapted ones survive and breed.

clue.text: In recompense, arranged for attendance everywhere

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are set out differently

parts.note: all twelve letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone gets paid back for turning up to everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In recompense' reads as a set phrase meaning 'as payment', which hides that both words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Omnipresence is the state of being present in all places at once, so being in attendance at every location.

clue.text: Impression is a success

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a feeling or perception
second meaning: a hit that causes great excitement

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a verdict on a mimic's act; the two halves are separate meanings of one word joined by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a physical or mental feeling, and also an event or person causing a public stir, a hit.

clue.text: Physicist in 90s, sprightly

indicators.note: sprightly means lively and bouncing about, so the letters jump into a new order

parts.note: the 90s written out in full

explanation.surface: A scientist still full of energy in extreme old age.
explanation.walkthrough: The numeral must be spelt out as a word before its letters can be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein was the theoretical scientist behind relativity, the best-known physicist of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Staves conferred extremely piously to represent elevated status, primarily?

definitions.text: Staves conferred extremely piously to represent elevated status, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily points to what comes first, so only the initial of each word counts

parts.words: Staves conferred extremely piously to represent elevated status
parts.note: the first letters of these eight words

explanation.surface: Ceremonial rods handed over with great reverence as symbols of high rank.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer while its eight initials spell it; the question mark flags that double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Sceptres are ornamental rods presented at coronations to a monarch as emblems of royal power and rank.

clue.text: Latest: nephew that is detained by nuns for causing trouble

parts.note: the latest thing is in, fashionable

indicators.note: someone detained is held inside, so one piece is kept within another

parts.note: a convent is a community of nuns
N is the abbreviation for nephew
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: The newest news: a young relative is being held by nuns for misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latest' looks like a news heading; it means fashionable. 'Nuns' stands for the building they live in, which holds the nephew and 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inconvenient creates difficulty or bother for someone, so it is a cause of trouble.

clue.text: Anglo-Saxon meeting with keen Spanish affirmation in old Italian town

parts.note: the initial letters of Anglo and Saxon
si is Spanish for yes, and an eager speaker says it twice

explanation.surface: An English traveller meets an enthusiastic Spaniard nodding yes in a historic Italian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' is why the Spanish yes is doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, the medieval birthplace of St Francis, so a historic place in Italy.

clue.text: Car, old sausage

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for a battered old car
second meaning: British slang for a sausage

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a banger is both a clapped-out car and a sausage, as in bangers and mash; 'old' belongs with the car.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the one word for a worn-out, noisy vehicle and for a fried pork link.

clue.text: Implausibly cheers up touring large tomb

indicators.note: to tour is to go all round something, so one piece travels around another
implausibly means in a way hard to believe, so the letters are not in a believable order

parts.note: the letters of both words
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing

explanation.surface: Visiting a huge burial monument somehow lifts someone's spirits, against all expectation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers up' reads as a verb phrase; it is the letters to rearrange, which then wrap around L.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepulchre is a stone burial chamber or vault, so another word for a tomb.

clue.text: This describes something healthier in the pub

definitions.note: a sentence about an adjective, not the adjective itself
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an adjective for food or drink low in calories
second meaning: the pub nearest home that a person regularly uses

explanation.surface: Someone orders the lighter option at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The British 'local' is your regular neighbourhood pub; split with a hyphen, the same letters are the label on diet products.
explanation.definitionFit: Lo-cal is shorthand for low-calorie, a label for slimming food, while a regular's nearest tavern is called their local.

clue.text: Lost in fantasies regularly, abstracted at first

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of abstracted

explanation.surface: A daydreamer drifts off into flights of fancy, absent-minded from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost in fantasies' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is the link, with the definition being just 'Lost'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at sea is an idiom for being confused or bewildered, so not knowing which way to turn.

clue.text: To some extent, fear a cheesy auricular annoyance

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only a portion of the following text is used

parts.note: runs from inside fear, across a, into cheesy

explanation.surface: Dreading some corny chat-up line that grates on the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auricular' means to do with the ear, so the definition is a pain in that organ.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is a pain inside the ear, and auricular is the formal adjective for things relating to the ear.

clue.text: Volunteering work repeatedly trendy: good

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
in means trendy, and repeatedly means it appears twice
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Doing unpaid charity work has become fashionable again and again, which is a good thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volunteering' looks like charity work; it means offering a view unasked.
explanation.definitionFit: To volunteer a remark is to offer it unprompted, and opining is offering one's view in just that way.

clue.text: Starters of niçoises: endives cored, stale, curl up

indicators.note: coring removes the middle, so the central letter of the word goes
starters come first, so each word supplies only its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of niçoises
the first letter of endives
taken as written; its middle letter A is removed

explanation.surface: A salad report: the endives, cored, are stale and curling at the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cored' sits beside 'endives' and looks as if it describes them, but it acts on 'stale'. A salade niçoise is a French salad with tuna, eggs and olives.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle snugly and comfortably, as a cat or child does when it curls up.

clue.text: Hide, hold back, becoming more emaciated

parts.note: an animal's hide is its skin

indicators.note: back means backwards, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to rein is to hold in check

explanation.surface: Someone hides and holds back from eating, and so grows thinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb, to conceal; it is the noun, an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Skinny means very thin, so its comparative describes someone thinner and bonier, closer to wasting away.
